title: Inverse Depth Scaling From Most Layers Being Similar
claim: Of three candidate ways stacked layers can use depth, the evidence supports redundant averaging of noisy estimates, not composition or smooth dynamics.
layout: 3 colored panels left-to-right, conclusion banner arrow beneath, green checkmark on last
description: Three rounded panels, pink, yellow and green, sit side by side. Each shows one regime for how an LLM uses its layers. The pink panel, Compositional Assembly, shows inputs at the top, a vertical stack of white pills (Layer 1 Syntax, Layer 2 Semantics, Layer 3 Reasoning) and gray arrows to outputs. Complex inputs pass through every layer and simple inputs skip down a bypass. The yellow panel, Procedural Assembly (discretization of smooth dynamics), plots state space with a smooth target curve from h0 to h_ell. Small gray arrows for each layer step follow the curve to the ideal final state. The green panel, Ensemble Averaging (law of large numbers), shows noisy zigzag layer arrows scattered around a straight line to an abstract input-output mapping. It carries the label L~1/depth and a large green checkmark. A gray banner arrow underneath states the conclusion. The eye goes first to the checkmark and the bold titles.
caption: Three regimes of how LLMs may utilize their layers.
abstract: Neural scaling laws relate loss to model size in large language models (LLMs), yet depth and width may contribute to performance differently, requiring more detailed studies. Here, we quantify how depth affects loss via analysis of LLMs and toy residual networks. We find loss scales inversely proportional to depth in LLMs, probably due to functionally similar layers reducing error through ensemble averaging rather than compositional learning or discretizing smooth dynamics. This regime is inefficient yet robust and may arise from the architectural bias of residual networks and target functions incompatible with smooth dynamics. The findings suggest that improving LLM efficiency may require architectural innovations to encourage compositional use of depth.
